klo: Evaluate whether organisational performance arrangements support the achievement of strategic priorities.
Define clear relationships between enterprise outcomes, leadership accountability and performance evidence.
Exercise consistent executive judgement on performance status and its strategic significance.
Interpret performance insight in ways that strengthen accountability, decision quality and organisational responsiveness.

sections.label: Facilitator Guide
sections.sub: Use this tab to orient yourself before each section. It contains purpose, timing, tone, and key facilitation questions for the full unit.

guidance: ◆ Unit Intent

Unit 6 bridges strategy and execution accountability. Many organisations have measurement systems but lack management systems. Participants should leave understanding the distinction — and knowing how to build the management side. The emphasis is on design thinking: how to construct a system that drives behaviour as well as tracking it. This is one of the more technical units in S2R® — keep the energy applied.
◆ Key Facilitation Questions
“In your organisation, are you measuring what happened — or managing what will happen next?”
“If your team stopped producing reports tomorrow, what decisions would you lose the ability to make?”
“Is your current PM system designed to generate compliance — or to build commitment?”
“Where in your organisation does measurement transparency break down? Who does not see their numbers?”
“When you review performance, are you looking at activity or at cumulative progress toward target?”
◆ Tone & Watch Points
Avoid: turning the FACES or EXECUTION frameworks into a compliance checklist. They are diagnostic and design tools.
Watch for: leaders who equate “we have a scorecard” with “we have a PM system.” Probe: “What happens after you look at the scorecard? What changes? Who decides what?”
The Solid Gold reframe (Rating 3 = Solid Gold) is intentional and often powerful. Bring it to life with an example of a consistent contributor who reliably delivers and is still overlooked.

sections.label: Section 1 · Awareness — What
sections.sub: Establishing the conceptual ground: what performance management actually is, how it differs from measurement, and the functional architecture that makes it work.
slo: Distinguish the management of performance from its measurement.
Exercise consistent judgement on performance status and the leadership response it requires.

parts.title: 1.1 — Measurement vs Management
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

Ask: “In your organisation, which comes first — the data collection system or the definition of success? How many reports exist that nobody acts on?” Most will recognise that measurement infrastructure was built first and management systems are retrofitted — or entirely absent.
content: Performance management and performance measurement are distinct disciplines. This distinction is the single most important conceptual anchor in Unit 6 — and the one most organisations get wrong.
Measurement answers: What happened? It is an input — data, results, scores, dashboards.
Management answers: What do we do about it? It is the leadership response that turns data into decisions, actions, and accountability.

Most organisations have built sophisticated measurement systems and mistakenly believe they have performance management systems. A measurement system without a management architecture produces reports. A management system converts those reports into movement.

Before any system is designed, leadership must be explicit about what success looks like. What are we trying to achieve? By when? At what level of quality or scale? Without this, measurement has no target and management has no compass.

Design the system for managing toward success. What conversations will we have? How often? Who is accountable? What decisions will be made, and by whom? The management architecture must exist before measurement is collected — otherwise data accumulates with no system to act on it.
Design the measurement tools that will feed the management system. What data do we need? How frequently? In what format? Measurement should serve the management conversations already defined.

Execute the management system using measurement data as the evidence base for conversations, interventions, recognition, and course correction. This is where most organisations start — collecting data before having a system to use it.

parts.title: 1.2 — The FACES Framework
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

Ask participants to rate their current PM system against each FACES dimension (1–5). Typical gap: most organisations score highest on “Create Measurement Transparency” (they have dashboards) and lowest on “Embed Shared Accountability” (accountability lives with the leader alone).
content: A complete performance management system serves five interconnected functions. These are simultaneous functions that every well-designed PM system must perform.

The PM system must reinforce a culture in which results matter, are visible, and are celebrated or addressed consistently. Culture is shaped by what gets measured, what gets discussed, and what gets rewarded. A PM system that avoids difficult conversations actively undermines results culture — no matter how sophisticated the dashboard.
Facilitation cue: “What does your PM system reward? Does it reward activity or results? Compliance or commitment?”

Every individual must see a clear line of sight between their daily work and the organisation’s strategic outcomes. Without this alignment, effort is misdirected. The PM system must decompose strategic outcomes into team and individual targets that are genuinely connected.

People perform at a higher level when they can see their own performance data and understand how it is calculated. Transparency ensures that the logic of measurement is understood and trusted. Hidden formulas and opaque scoring destroy confidence in the PM system.

The PM system must embed accountability as a shared expectation. Shared accountability means teams co-own the results — they participate in setting targets, understand the evidence, and are part of the intervention process. Systems that locate accountability solely in the leader create dependency and fragility.

The PM system must identify what performance reveals about capability gaps, development needs, and growth trajectories. Performance data is a development signal as well as an accountability score. Leaders who use PM data only for ratings miss its most powerful application: designing targeted development that improves future performance.

parts.title: 1.3 — The Three Sights of Progress
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

A common gap: organisations measure Sight 1 and Sight 2 rigorously but treat Sight 3 as a subjective add-on. Surface this: “In your current system, what weight does behavioural alignment carry in the final performance rating? Is it measured formally or informally?”
content: A well-designed PM system tracks performance across three distinct categories. Each sight provides a different angle on whether the organisation is progressing toward its strategic intent. At the individual level, weightings are assigned according to role and function.
Strategic OKRs directly connected to the organisation’s multi-year strategy. This sight asks: Are we making progress on the things that matter most for where we are going?
Typically 30–50% at senior levels; lower for frontline roles. Reviewed quarterly with executive visibility.
Departmental KPIs tracking the operational engine — efficiency, output, quality, and service delivery. This sight asks: Are our operations performing at the standard required to sustain strategy?
Typically 30–50% across most role levels; highest for frontline and specialist roles. Reviewed monthly or fortnightly.

How individuals demonstrate the organisation’s values and leadership behaviours — assessed through 360° feedback and peer observation. How results are achieved matters as much as what results are achieved.
Typically 20–40% across role levels; higher for leadership and customer-facing roles. Assessed bi-annually or annually via structured 360°.

parts.title: 1.4 — The 1–5 Rating Scale
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

The Solid Gold reframe generates significant discussion. Invite reflection: “What message has your body language, tone, or incentive system sent to people rated 3?” Also surface the Rating 5 accountability point: “In the last three years, how many people received a Rating 5? What happened to them afterwards?”
content: A rating scale only has value if it is consistently understood and each rating triggers a defined leadership response.
Leadership response: Immediate PIP within 30 days
Definition: Performance is significantly below the minimum standard. Output is insufficient, quality is unacceptable, or behaviour is actively damaging.

Leadership response: Immediate intervention. A formal performance improvement plan within 30 days. Weekly check-ins. Assess whether the gap is capability, motivation, or role-fit. A Rating 1 sustained beyond 60 days without visible movement is a role-fit decision.
Definition: Performance is below the expected standard in one or more significant areas. The individual shows some capability but has consistent gaps in output, quality, or behaviour.

Leadership response: Structured development plan with specific targets and milestones. Fortnightly check-ins. Clear articulation of the standard required to achieve a Rating 3 by the next review cycle.

Definition: Performance fully meets the standard expected for this role, at this level, in this context. Output is consistent, quality is reliable, behaviour is aligned. This is exactly what the role requires.

The Solid Gold Reframe: Most PM systems implicitly treat a Rating 3 as mediocre — a design flaw that erodes morale and incentivises performative overreach. A Rating 3 is “Solid Gold”: a person who reliably delivers and represents the backbone of execution in any high-performing organisation.

Leadership response: Recognition of consistent contribution. Exploration of growth aspirations — without implying that remaining at a 3 is a failure. Many exceptional contributors are sustainably and appropriately at a 3.
Leadership response: Stretch opportunities; retention investment
Definition: Performance consistently goes beyond what the role requires. The individual proactively adds value, solves problems beyond their mandate, and elevates the team. A Rating 4 is a pattern.

Leadership response: Explicit recognition and visibility with senior leadership. Conversation about stretch opportunities, expanded scope, or accelerated development. Failure to invest in a sustained Rating 4 is a retention risk.

Definition: Performance is transformational within the context of the role. The individual exceeds their own targets and demonstrably elevates others and advances the organisation. A Rating 5 is rare and must be ratified.

Leadership response: A Rating 5 carries a leadership obligation — increased scope, a promotion discussion, a compensation review, or a high-impact project assignment. A Rating 5 acknowledged verbally with no structural follow-through is a trust-destroying event. The individual will note that outstanding performance produced no change — and will adjust their effort accordingly.

sections.label: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
sections.sub: Understanding the structural logic of how performance management connects strategy to individual action, and why most PM systems fail to make that connection.
slo: Define how performance management connects enterprise outcomes to individual accountability.
Evaluate whether current performance arrangements build compliance or commitment.

parts.title: 2.1 — PM as the Execution Bridge
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

Ask participants to identify which bridge function is most underdeveloped. “Where does your strategy most commonly leak? At decomposition, at defining success, at the rhythm, or at the quality of the conversation?”
content: A performance management system performs four critical bridging functions between strategy and execution. When any one is missing, the bridge develops a structural gap — and strategy leaks through it.

Strategy lives at the enterprise level. PM translates it into progressively smaller, actionable units: enterprise outcomes → business unit contributions → team targets → individual responsibilities. Without decomposition, strategy remains a declaration and never becomes a task.

The PM system must make explicit what “success” looks like at each level — as a measurable, observable outcome with defined evidence. When the logic of success is ambiguous, individuals define it for themselves — and those self-definitions are rarely aligned.

Strategy operates on an annual or multi-year timeline. Individual performance operates daily. The PM system must establish a structured rhythm connecting these timelines. Without rhythm, PM becomes an isolated event.
Progress per Period = (End Target − Baseline) ÷ Number of Periods
This establishes the expected incremental progress in each review period, creating a visible trajectory through the year.

Data without conversation is noise. The PM system must structure the dialogue that turns performance data into decisions. Define: who speaks, how frequently, about what, and with what authority to decide. The quality of the PM conversation is the quality of the PM system.

parts.title: 2.2 — Compliance vs Commitment Architecture
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

Most organisations have compliance systems that use commitment language. The test: “When performance data shows underperformance, what is the first instinct of the leader — to fix the person, or to understand the system?” Invite leaders to identify the one structural change that would shift their system most decisively toward commitment.
content: Every PM system is built on one of two architectural orientations: compliance or commitment. The choice is rarely made explicitly — but it is always made. The six dimensions below reveal which architecture is currently operating.
Purpose | Ensure minimum standards are met and deviations corrected | Generate shared ownership of results and continuous improvement
Ownership | Leader holds accountability; team is subject to it | Team co-owns accountability; leader facilitates
Tone | Assessment and judgement; hierarchical | Inquiry and problem-solving; collaborative
Underperformance | Consequence and control | Understanding root cause; co-designing recovery
Motivation | Avoiding negative consequence | Intrinsic meaning; shared pride in progress
PM experience | Anxiety-producing; done to the individual | Energy-generating; done with the individual

parts.title: 2.3 — Rules of the Game
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

The most common failure in Step 1 is the evidence standard. Ask: “If two managers each gave someone a Rating 4, would they be using the same evidence?” Step 2 often breaks down at “Assign Ownership” — most cascade conversations end with team-level accountability that no single person is actually responsible for.
content: Before performance can be managed, the rules must be established and understood by everyone expected to play. Two steps structure this process.
Rating Scale: Agree the 1–5 scale, definitions of each level, and evidence required to differentiate between them. Ambiguity here creates inconsistency and destroys trust.
Performance Thresholds: Define the minimum acceptable standard for each role. What constitutes a sustained Rating 2 requiring intervention?
Evidence Standards: Determine what counts as evidence of performance — output volume, quality metrics, peer feedback, customer satisfaction. Must be explicit.
Review Routine: Establish the cadence: how frequently performance is reviewed, in what format, with what participants. A routine that is skipped destroys PM system credibility.

Verify the Data: Before any cascade conversation, confirm that data is accurate, current, and consistently interpreted. A cascade built on flawed data produces misaligned targets and erodes trust in the entire PM system.
Assign Ownership: Every metric must have a single named owner. Collective ownership without individual ownership is shared irresponsibility.

Focus on Learning: The cascade conversation is a learning conversation as well as target-setting. What does this target reveal about capability requirements? What barriers must be removed? Leaders who conduct the cascade purely as a negotiation miss its most important function.

parts.title: 2.4 — Leader vs Team: A Critical Distinction
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

This is a powerful reframe for leaders who conflate team busyness with strategic progress. “Is your current PM review looking at your team’s activities — or at your cumulative outcome trajectory? When last did you review whether your team’s activities are actually producing the outcomes the strategy requires?”
content: One of the most frequently misunderstood aspects of performance management is the distinction between how a team is measured and how its leader is measured. Conflating the two creates misaligned incentives and obscures accountability.
Focus | Activities, outputs, and behaviours within the review period | Cumulative outcome trajectory across the full performance cycle
Time horizon | Current period: what was done, how it was done | End-of-cycle: are we on track to reach the target by year-end?
Evidence | Deliverable completion, quality scores, behavioural indicators | Cumulative progress calculation; gap to target; trend direction
Review frequency | Monthly / quarterly | Quarterly / bi-annually

The practical implication: A team can complete every planned activity on time (strong team performance) while the leader’s cumulative outcome trajectory is still off track (weak leadership performance). The leader is accountable for ensuring tasks are producing the outcomes the strategy requires.

sections.label: Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where
sections.sub: Extending PM architecture to the enterprise level: how executive teams align their measurement signals, where execution gaps emerge, and how industry context is shifting.
slo: Recognise each executive role’s contribution to the evidence of enterprise progress.
Evaluate the execution gaps that prevent performance arrangements from supporting strategic priorities.

parts.title: 3.1 — The Alignment Brigade
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

Ask the executive team to independently write down the top three enterprise performance priorities right now — then compare answers. The degree of divergence is a direct measure of Alignment Brigade dysfunction. “If your executive team cannot agree on the top three, how does the organisation below you know where to focus?”
content: At the enterprise level, the performance management system sits in the executive team. The C-suite is, collectively, the organisation’s measurement alignment system. When the executive team is not aligned on what they are measuring, why, and what they are doing about it, the enterprise PM system is structurally broken regardless of the tools in place.

The Alignment Brigade concept recognises that each executive function carries a unique measurement responsibility — a “hot zone” of the enterprise that they are best positioned to track, interpret, and act upon. When these hot zones are integrated through a shared cadence and common language, the executive team becomes a precision measurement system. When they operate independently, they produce competing narratives of organisational performance.

The critical question for any executive team: “When we look at the same performance data, do we interpret it from the same perspective — or from the perspective of our function? And when the data tells us to act, do we act as a system or as a collection of functions?”

parts.title: 3.2 — CXO Hot Zones
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

Invite participants to work through their own role card first, then two closely related roles. Key question: “In your last executive performance review, were all ten hot zones represented? What does the absence of a hot zone from the executive PM conversation produce in the organisation below?”
content: Each executive function owns a distinct hot zone in the enterprise PM architecture. Click a role to explore its measurement responsibility and contribution to the collective progress signal.

CEO — Enterprise Visibility: The CEO holds the integrated view of whether the organisation as a whole is on trajectory. The CEO’s PM role is to ensure the executive team is interpreting performance coherently and that the collective response is coordinated. The CEO is the only function with authority to enforce measurement alignment across all hot zones. When CEO PM visibility is absent, each function optimises its own metric at the expense of enterprise coherence.

CFO — Financial Signals: The CFO interprets the financial performance signal: revenue, cost, margin, liquidity, and capital efficiency. In the PM context, the CFO translates financial data into strategic resource allocation signals — identifying where investment is producing returns and where it is absorbed without output. When CFO PM insight is isolated, financial data becomes a constraint and loses its value as a strategic navigation tool.

COO — Execution Rhythm: The COO tracks the execution engine: throughput, cycle times, operational quality, and delivery consistency. The COO ensures operational performance rhythm is matched to strategic demand — the engine is running in the right direction at the right speed. When COO PM is activity-focused, the organisation confuses motion with progress.

CHRO — Capability & Behaviour: The CHRO tracks the capability and behaviour signal: talent pipeline health, performance distribution, leadership effectiveness, and cultural alignment. The CHRO ensures the organisation has the human capability to execute the strategy — and that behaviour is aligned to values as well as outcomes. When CHRO PM data is absent from executive reviews, capability gaps become execution crises.

CTO/CIO — System Enablement: The CTO/CIO tracks system enablement: technology performance, digital capability, data quality, and system reliability. This function ensures technology is an execution accelerator. Poor system performance is a PM variable — it directly affects what people can deliver. When technology performance is excluded from PM reviews, teams are held accountable for gaps caused by system failures.

CMO — Market Signal: The CMO tracks brand perception, customer acquisition costs, pipeline health, campaign performance, and market share trajectory. The CMO provides the leading indicators of future revenue — the signal that tells the enterprise whether the market is responding to the strategy. When CMO PM data is lagged, the enterprise acts on market signals that are already 3–6 months old.

CCO — Revenue Velocity: The CCO tracks win rates, deal cycle times, customer retention, revenue per customer, and commercial pipeline conversion. The CCO translates commercial activity into revenue trajectory signals connecting market position to financial performance. When CCO PM is focused on activity, the organisation mistakes effort for momentum.

CPO — Supply Reliability: The CPO tracks supply reliability, product pipeline health, vendor performance, and input cost management. The CPO ensures the supply and product infrastructure can reliably support execution — that the organisation can deliver what it has committed to deliver. When CPO PM is reactive, supply disruptions become execution crises that consume leadership capacity.

CRO — Risk & Governance: The CRO tracks regulatory compliance, risk appetite alignment, incident frequency, and control effectiveness. The CRO ensures strategic ambition is pursued within a coherent risk framework — enabling bold action without reckless exposure. When CRO PM is siloed, risk appetite is interpreted differently across functions, creating asymmetric exposure.

CSO — Strategic Coherence: The CSO tracks whether the organisation’s current activities, resource allocation, and performance trajectory are aligned to its multi-year strategic intent. The CSO provides the strategic integrity check — ensuring operational performance is not winning at the expense of strategic positioning. When CSO PM is absent, operational urgency systematically erodes strategic intent over time.

parts.title: 3.3 — The Three Execution Gaps
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

Ask the group to vote (anonymously if needed) on which Execution Gap is most present in their organisation. In most executive contexts, Gap 1 and Gap 3 will dominate. The discussion about why these gaps persist despite being well understood is where the real facilitation work happens. The answer is usually political: fixing the gap requires someone to give up control of a metric or accept shared accountability they have historically resisted.
content: Three structural gaps account for the majority of PM system failures at the enterprise level. Each gap is a predictable consequence of a specific design flaw.

Different functions or leaders are using different definitions of what constitutes progress — finance says margin, operations says throughput, sales says pipeline. Without a unified definition of progress at the enterprise level, each function optimises its own metric at the expense of collective momentum.

Intervention: Establish an enterprise progress definition in the executive PM session. Agree on the three to five metrics that, if achieved, confirm the strategy is working. Everything else is a supporting indicator.

The organisation is systematically not measuring something that matters. Common blind spots: quality of cross-functional collaboration, health of the leadership pipeline, customer experience at key touchpoints. What is not measured is not managed — and eventually becomes a crisis.
Intervention: Map the current measurement system against the Three Sights of Progress. Ask: “What would we need to see to know our strategy is working before the financial results confirm it?”

The incentive structure rewards behaviour inconsistent with the strategic intent. Leaders are rewarded for short-term financial performance while the strategy requires long-term capability investment. People follow the incentives. When incentives and strategy diverge, strategy loses.

Intervention: Audit the current incentive structure against strategic priorities. Redesign to reward the behaviours the strategy actually requires. Where are incentives producing the wrong behaviour? Which strategic priorities have no incentive attached?

parts.title: 3.4 — The Continuous PM Shift
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

Invite participants to locate their organisation on the spectrum from traditional (annual, rating-centric, individual) to leading-edge (continuous, development-centric, team-integrated). “Where are you now — and where do you need to be in three years?”
content: 41% of organisations have moved to real-time or near-real-time feedback systems, replacing annual or bi-annual performance review cycles with continuous check-in models. This shift reflects a fundamental change in how high-performing organisations understand the relationship between feedback and performance.

The annual performance review is being supplemented or replaced by structured quarterly conversations, monthly check-ins, and continuous pulse feedback. The shift recognises that annual feedback is too infrequent to change behaviour and too delayed to be developmental.

Leading organisations are shifting from the rating (a backward-looking judgement) to development planning (a forward-looking investment). The rating becomes an input to development. Associated with higher engagement, stronger retention, and more rapid capability improvement.

As organisations become more cross-functional, individual performance ratings are being complemented by team performance assessments. Most outcomes require coordinated contribution. Organisations that exclusively measure individual performance create hidden disincentives for collaboration.

sections.label: Section 4 · Integration — Collective
sections.sub: Synthesising awareness, intelligence, and context into an integrated enterprise PM design: the collective progress signal, three elements of enterprise PM, and the EXECUTION framework.
slo: Define a shared enterprise signal of progress that anchors executive judgement.
Interpret cumulative progress to judge performance status and its strategic significance.

parts.title: 4.1 — The Collective Progress Signal
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

In most organisations, executive PM conversations are dominated by Traction questions with insufficient time for Balance and Intervention. “When last did your executive team have an Execution Balance conversation? When last did a performance review result in an explicit, named Intervention decision with an accountable owner and a deadline?”
content: At the integration level, the executive team converges on a single shared signal: are we collectively making progress toward our strategic intent? This Collective Progress Signal anchors three categories of executive question.
“Are our current activities generating the progress we expected?”

This assesses whether the execution engine is producing results at the rate and quality the strategy requires. Execution Traction questions are the most frequent in a well-functioning executive PM rhythm — they are the standing agenda item in every performance review. The risk: if only Traction questions are asked, the executive team optimises for current-period efficiency and loses sight of cumulative trajectory.
“Are we investing our resources in the right proportions across our strategic priorities?”

This steps back from individual metric performance to assess whether the portfolio of activity is balanced. High-performing organisations regularly discover that 80% of their resource is concentrated on the priority representing 30% of their strategic value — because that priority is most familiar or most politically visible.
“Where must we intervene — with resources, decisions, or leadership attention — to prevent a performance gap from becoming a strategic failure?”

The most consequential question in the executive PM dialogue. It moves from analysis to action: a specific decision about where leadership will direct energy, resources, or authority to recover a trajectory that is currently off track. Organisations that defer intervention decisions until the gap is irreversible have compliance PM systems masquerading as management systems.

parts.title: 4.2 — Three Elements of Enterprise PM Design
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

The Cumulative Progress formula is a practical tool participants can apply immediately. Ask them to identify one current strategic priority and calculate their cumulative progress percentage. This frequently reveals that organisations are further behind their end-of-cycle target than their most recent period improvement suggests — a critical insight for Intervention decisions.
content: A complete enterprise PM design integrates three elements. Each answers a different question at a different time horizon. All three must be present for the PM system to function as a genuine management architecture.

Reporting Cadence defines the structured rhythm: when performance is reviewed, by whom, and with what mandate. Without a defined cadence, performance management reverts to crisis management — leaders look at the numbers only when something goes wrong.
Daily: Frontline operational metrics; team leader visibility
Weekly: Departmental progress checks; emerging issues flagged
Monthly: Functional performance review; Periodic Measure analysis
Quarterly: Enterprise PM review; Cumulative Progress assessment; Intervention decisions
Annually: Full PM cycle review; rating calibration; system redesign

Periodic Measures are the performance data points collected and reviewed within each reporting period. They answer: What happened in this period? What is our current performance level? Periodic Measures must be:
Current: Reflecting performance within the most recent review period
Comparable: Measurable against the same standard as previous periods
Actionable: Capable of informing a decision or intervention in the next period
A Periodic Measure that is only collected, never acted on, is a reporting cost with no management value.

Cumulative Progress is the most strategically significant element and the most frequently absent. It answers: Across the full performance cycle, how far have we moved from where we started toward where we need to be?
Example: Complaint resolution baseline = 48 hrs, target = 12 hrs, current = 40 hrs.
This formula reveals whether the organisation is on trajectory to reach its target by end of cycle. A single-period improvement can mask a cumulative trajectory that is far behind target.

parts.title: 4.3 — The EXECUTION Framework
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

Run EXECUTION as a self-scoring diagnostic: ask each participant to rate their current PM system 1–5 against each letter. Compare scores across the group. “Which principle scored lowest? What is the cost of that gap? What is the one change that would address it?” This becomes the bridge into the Application section.
content: The EXECUTION framework synthesises the nine design principles of a high-quality enterprise PM system. Each letter represents a principle that, when absent, creates a specific and predictable PM failure mode. Use as a design tool and a diagnostic.
The PM system must be anchored to enterprise strategy. Every metric should be traceable to a strategic outcome. The enterprise intent is the filter through which all PM design decisions are made.

Every individual must see a clear line of sight from their daily work to enterprise strategy. Line-of-sight is the translation mechanism that makes strategy personal. Without it, individuals execute their role description and lose sight of the strategy.

Performance assessments must be grounded in defined, agreed evidence. Evidence-based measurement protects the integrity of the PM system and builds trust. Without it, ratings are subjective and disputes are inevitable.

Accountability for results must be shared across the team and organisation. Collective ownership means everyone with a contribution to an outcome has a stake in its measurement and a responsibility for its achievement.
The PM system must measure outcomes — the actual change produced. A team can be 100% active while producing 0% of the required outcome. Leaders must measure impact.

The logic by which performance is calculated, rated, and rewarded must be transparent to everyone subject to it. Hidden formulas and opaque scoring destroy confidence in the system and generate cynicism that undermines the entire PM architecture.

The incentive structure must reward the behaviours and outcomes the strategy requires. Misaligned incentives are one of the most reliable predictors of strategy failure. When what gets rewarded diverges from what the strategy needs, people follow the incentive — this is a design failure.

PM must be an ongoing rhythm. An annual review cycle produces information too infrequently to inform in-year course correction. The review rhythm must be consistent and embedded in the operational calendar so that PM is the way work is managed.

The ultimate function of a PM system is navigation: using performance data, collectively interpreted, to make better decisions about where to go and how to get there. A PM system that collects data but does not generate collective insight is a reporting system dressed as management.

sections.label: Section 5 · Application — In Practice
sections.h2: MyHealth Live Portal — PM Design Simulation
sections.sub: Applying the full unit to a realistic case: designing the performance management architecture for a hospital chain launching a digital patient engagement portal.
slo: Design performance arrangements that link enterprise outcomes, leadership accountability and performance evidence.
Interpret progress data to strengthen accountability, decision quality and responsiveness.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Simulation Setup

Briefing: Present the MyHealth Live Portal context. Participants work individually through each task first (15 min), then compare outputs at the table. The debrief should focus on design choices — there is no single correct answer. The richness is in the reasoning.
Suggested timing: Individual work 15 min → Table discussion 15 min → Group debrief 15 min. Tasks 5 and 6 can be combined for groups that move quickly through the earlier tasks.

parts.title: 5.1 — Case Context: MyHealth Live Portal
content: Organisation: A hospital chain operating 12 facilities across three regions. The board has approved a digital transformation initiative: the MyHealth Live Portal, a patient-facing platform enabling online appointment booking, real-time test results, and direct clinical communication.
Strategic Context: The portal is a strategic priority for the next 18 months. Three strategic outcomes have been defined by the executive team:
Reduce patient complaint resolution time: 48 hrs → 12 hrs
Key Result: Portal-based complaint submission and tracking live in all 12 facilities within 6 months; average resolution time below 12 hours within 12 months.
Reduce clinical referral decision time: 10 days → 3 days
Key Result: Digital referral pathway active for 80% of non-urgent referral types within 9 months; average decision time below 3 days within 15 months.
Baseline: 30% of cases involve cross-facility input Target: 70%
Key Result: Shared case management module live within 6 months; cross-facility consultation rate at or above 70% within 18 months.

parts.title: 5.2 — Task 1 · PM Scorecard Architecture
content: Design a PM Scorecard for the Chief Operations Officer. The scorecard must integrate all Three Sights of Progress and reflect the organisation’s strategic outcomes.
Identify three to five metrics for each of the Three Sights (Strategic OKRs, Operational KPIs, Behavioural/Values Alignment)
Assign a weighting to each Sight that reflects the COO’s role and strategic context
Confirm that at least one metric in the Strategic OKR category is directly traceable to the MyHealth Live Portal strategic outcomes
Identify the single metric you consider the most critical lead indicator of overall execution traction

parts.title: 5.3 — Task 2 · Scoring Logic Design
content: Design the scoring logic for Outcome 1 (complaint resolution time). The logic must define how performance is translated into a 1–5 rating.
Define what performance level earns each rating from 1 to 5 for the complaint resolution time metric
Specify what evidence is required to confirm each rating (the number and how it is verified)
Identify any contextual factors that might legitimately affect the rating (e.g. facility size, patient volume)
Describe the leadership response that each rating should trigger in the monthly review

parts.title: 5.4 — Task 3 · Baseline Simulation
content: Using the Cumulative Progress formula, calculate the current cumulative progress % for each strategic outcome. Assume the following data at month 6 of an 18-month cycle:
Outcome 1: Current = 40 hrs | Baseline = 48 hrs | Target = 12 hrs
Outcome 2: Current = 8 days | Baseline = 10 days | Target = 3 days
Expected progress at month 6 of an 18-month cycle = 33%. Which outcome is most at risk? What Execution Intervention would you recommend?

parts.title: 5.5 — Task 4 · Reporting Cadence Design
content: Design the full Reporting Cadence for the MyHealth Live Portal PM system, spanning from daily operational tracking through to the quarterly executive review.
For each cadence level (daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly), specify: what is reviewed, by whom, and what decisions can be made at that level
Identify which CXO Hot Zones must be present at the quarterly executive review and what each must bring
Design the escalation rule: at what threshold does a monthly performance gap automatically trigger a quarterly Execution Intervention discussion?
How would the cadence need to change at month 12 if Outcome 3 is still below 50%?

parts.title: 5.6 — Task 5 · Periodic Measures Selection
content: Select the Periodic Measures that will be tracked monthly across the three strategic outcomes. Each measure must be current, comparable, and actionable.
Identify three to four Periodic Measures for each strategic outcome; specify: what it tracks, how frequently collected, who owns the data, what action it triggers if it deteriorates
Identify one leading indicator for each outcome — a measure that signals future performance before the outcome metric itself changes
Identify any measures that would represent a Measurement Blind Spot if excluded

content: PM is the leadership response to measurement. The correct sequence: define success, design the management system, design the measurement infrastructure, then manage using data.

PM is an execution bridge with four functions: decomposing the big picture, defining the logic of success, calibrating the rhythm, and structuring the dialogue. The architecture choice — compliance vs commitment — shapes every conversation.
The executive team is the organisation’s measurement alignment system. Each CXO hot zone contributes a distinct signal. The Three Execution Gaps explain most PM failures at enterprise level.
The Collective Progress Signal anchors three executive question types: Traction, Balance, Intervention. Cumulative Progress calculation reveals whether the trajectory will reach target.

“A performance management system that only measures has not yet become a management system. The moment measurement becomes the basis for a decision, a conversation, and an accountable intervention — that is the moment execution begins.”

sections.label: Section 1 · Awareness — What
sections.sub: Establishing the conceptual ground: what performance management actually is, how it differs from measurement, and the functional architecture that makes it work.
slo: Distinguish the management of performance from its measurement.
Exercise consistent judgement on performance status and the leadership response it requires.

parts.title: 1.1 — Measurement vs Management
content: Performance management and performance measurement are distinct disciplines. This is one of the most important distinctions in strategy execution — and one most organisations get wrong.
Measurement answers: What happened? It is the data — results, dashboards, scores.
Management answers: What do we do about it? It is the leadership response that turns data into decisions, actions, and accountability.

Most organisations have sophisticated measurement systems and believe they have performance management systems. A measurement system without a management architecture produces reports. A management system converts those reports into movement.

Before any system is designed, be explicit about what success looks like. What are you trying to achieve? By when? At what level of quality or scale? Without this, measurement has no target and management has no compass.

Design the system for managing toward success. What conversations will you have? How often? Who is accountable? What decisions will be made? The management architecture must exist before measurement is collected — otherwise data accumulates with no system to act on it.
Design the measurement tools that feed the management system. What data do you need? How frequently? In what format? Measurement should serve the management conversations already defined.

Execute the management system using measurement data as the evidence base for conversations, interventions, recognition, and course correction. Most organisations start here — collecting data before having a system to use it. This is the most common PM design failure.

parts.title: 1.2 — The FACES Framework
content: A complete performance management system serves five interconnected functions simultaneously.

The PM system must reinforce a culture in which results matter, are visible, and are consistently celebrated or addressed. Culture is shaped by what gets measured, discussed, and rewarded. A PM system that avoids difficult conversations actively undermines results culture — regardless of how sophisticated the dashboard.

Every individual must see a clear line of sight between their daily work and the organisation’s strategic outcomes. Without this alignment, effort is misdirected. The PM system must decompose strategic outcomes into team and individual targets that are genuinely connected.

People perform at a higher level when they can see their own performance data and understand how it is calculated. Transparency ensures the logic of measurement is understood and trusted. Hidden formulas and opaque scoring destroy confidence in the PM system.

Accountability must be a shared expectation. Shared accountability means co-owning the results — participating in target-setting, understanding the evidence, and being part of the intervention process. Systems that locate accountability solely in the leader create dependency and fragility.

The PM system must identify what performance reveals about capability gaps, development needs, and growth trajectories. Performance data is a development signal as well as an accountability score. Leaders who use PM data only for ratings miss its most powerful application: designing development that improves future performance.
Rate your current PM system against each FACES function (1–5). Where is the highest gap? What would closing it change?
Biggest gap & what closing it would change
prompts: ✎ Reflection — FACES Diagnostic Rate your current PM system against each FACES function (1–5). Where is the highest gap? What would closing it change? FFoster a Results Culture AAlign Individual Performance CCreate Measurement Transparency EEmbed Shared Accountability SSupport Continuous Development Biggest gap & what closing it would change — The biggest FACES gap is… and closing it would change…

✎ Reflection — FACES Diagnostic Rate your current PM system against each FACES function (1–5). Where is the highest gap? What would closing it change? FFoster a Results Culture AAlign Individual Performance CCreate Measurement Transparency EEmbed Shared Accountability SSupport Continuous Development Biggest gap & what closing it would change

parts.title: 1.3 — The Three Sights of Progress
content: A well-designed PM system tracks performance across three distinct categories. Each sight provides a different angle on whether the organisation is progressing toward its strategic intent.
Strategic OKRs directly connected to the organisation’s multi-year strategy. Asks: Are we making progress on what matters most for where we are going?
30–50% at senior levels. Lower for frontline roles. Reviewed quarterly with executive visibility.
Departmental KPIs tracking the operational engine — efficiency, output, quality, and service delivery. Asks: Are operations performing at the standard required to sustain strategy?
30–50% across most role levels. Highest for frontline and specialist roles. Reviewed monthly or fortnightly.

How individuals demonstrate the organisation’s values and leadership behaviours — assessed through 360° feedback and peer observation. How results are achieved matters as much as what results are achieved.
20–40% across role levels. Higher for leadership and customer-facing roles. Assessed bi-annually via structured 360°.

parts.title: 1.4 — The 1–5 Rating Scale
content: A rating scale only has value if it is consistently understood and every rating triggers a defined leadership response. The scale below defines each level and its required response.
Response: Immediate performance improvement plan within 30 days

Performance is significantly below the minimum standard. Output is insufficient, quality is unacceptable, or behaviour is actively damaging. A Rating 1 sustained beyond 60 days without visible movement is a role-fit decision.
Response: Structured development plan with fortnightly check-ins

Performance is below the expected standard in one or more significant areas. The individual shows some capability but has consistent gaps in output, quality, or behaviour. The standard required to achieve a Rating 3 must be explicitly defined and communicated.

Performance fully meets the standard expected for this role, at this level, in this context. Output is consistent, quality is reliable, behaviour is aligned. A Rating 3 is Solid Gold — the person who reliably delivers and represents the backbone of execution in any high-performing organisation. The leadership response must reflect this: recognition.
Response: Stretch opportunities and retention investment

Performance consistently goes beyond what the role requires. The individual proactively adds value, solves problems beyond their mandate, and elevates the team. A Rating 4 is a pattern. Failure to invest in a sustained Rating 4 is a retention risk.
Response: Mandatory structural follow-through (promotion, scope, compensation)

Performance is transformational within the context of the role. The individual exceeds their own targets and demonstrably elevates others. A Rating 5 is rare and must be ratified. A Rating 5 acknowledged verbally with no structural follow-through is a trust-destroying event.

Thinking about your current team or role: which rating most accurately reflects the performance standard you are measuring toward? What does the leadership response to that rating look like in practice?
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Your Rating Experience Thinking about your current team or role: which rating most accurately reflects the performance standard you are measuring toward? What does the leadership response to that rating look like in practice? — My reflection on the rating scale and how it applies to my current context...

sections.label: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
sections.sub: Understanding the structural logic of how performance management connects strategy to individual action, and why most PM systems fail to make that connection.
slo: Define how performance management connects enterprise outcomes to individual accountability.
Evaluate whether current performance arrangements build compliance or commitment.

parts.title: 2.1 — PM as the Execution Bridge
content: A performance management system performs four critical bridging functions between strategy and execution. When any one is missing, the bridge develops a structural gap — and strategy leaks through it.

Strategy lives at enterprise level. PM translates it into progressively smaller, actionable units: enterprise outcomes → business unit contributions → team targets → individual responsibilities. Without decomposition, strategy remains a declaration and never becomes a task.

The PM system must make explicit what “success” looks like at each level — as a measurable, observable outcome with defined evidence. When the logic of success is ambiguous, individuals define it for themselves — and those self-definitions are rarely aligned.

Strategy operates on an annual or multi-year timeline. Individual performance operates daily. The PM system must establish a structured rhythm connecting these timelines. Without rhythm, PM becomes an isolated event.
Progress per Period = (End Target − Baseline) ÷ Number of Periods
This establishes the expected incremental progress in each review period — creating a visible trajectory through the year.

Data without conversation is noise. The PM system must structure the dialogue that turns performance data into decisions. Define: who speaks, how frequently, about what, and with what authority to decide. The quality of the PM conversation is the quality of the PM system.
Which of the four bridge functions is most underdeveloped in your organisation? Where does your strategy most commonly leak?
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Your Weakest Bridge Which of the four bridge functions is most underdeveloped in your organisation? Where does your strategy most commonly leak? — The bridge function most underdeveloped in my organisation is... Strategy leaks most often at...

parts.title: 2.2 — Compliance vs Commitment Architecture
content: Every PM system is built on one of two architectural orientations. The choice is rarely made explicitly — but it is always made. The six dimensions below reveal which architecture is currently operating in your organisation.
Purpose | Ensure minimum standards; correct deviations | Generate shared ownership; continuous improvement
Ownership | Leader holds accountability; team is subject to it | Team co-owns accountability; leader facilitates
Tone | Assessment and judgement; hierarchical | Inquiry and problem-solving; collaborative
Underperformance | Consequence and control | Understanding root cause; co-designing recovery
Motivation | Avoiding negative consequence | Intrinsic meaning; shared pride in progress
Experience | Anxiety-producing; done to the individual | Energy-generating; done with the individual
Where would you honestly place your current PM system on the spectrum from compliance to commitment? What is the single structural change that would shift it most decisively?
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Your Architecture Where would you honestly place your current PM system on the spectrum from compliance to commitment? What is the single structural change that would shift it most decisively? — My current PM architecture is closer to... because... The one structural change that would shift it: ...

parts.title: 2.3 — Rules of the Game
content: Before performance can be managed, the rules must be established and understood by everyone expected to play.
Rating ScaleAgree the 1–5 scale, definitions of each level, and evidence required to differentiate between them. Ambiguity here creates inconsistency and destroys trust.
Performance ThresholdsDefine the minimum acceptable standard for each role. What constitutes a sustained Rating 2 requiring intervention?
Evidence StandardsDetermine what counts as evidence of performance — output volume, quality metrics, peer feedback, customer satisfaction. Must be explicit.
Review RoutineEstablish the cadence: how frequently, in what format, with what participants. A routine that is skipped destroys PM system credibility.
Verify the DataBefore any cascade conversation, confirm data is accurate, current, and consistently interpreted. A cascade built on flawed data produces misaligned targets.
Assign OwnershipEvery metric must have a single named owner. Collective ownership without individual ownership is shared irresponsibility.

Focus on LearningThe cascade conversation is a learning conversation as well as target-setting. What does this target reveal about capability requirements? What barriers must be removed? Leaders who conduct the cascade purely as a negotiation miss its most important function.

parts.title: 2.4 — Leader vs Team: A Critical Distinction
content: One of the most frequently misunderstood aspects of PM is the distinction between how a team is measured and how its leader is measured.
Measured on | Activities, outputs, behaviours within the period | Cumulative outcome trajectory across the full cycle
Time horizon | Current period: what was done, how it was done | End-of-cycle: are we on track to reach the target?
Evidence | Deliverable completion, quality scores, behaviours | Cumulative progress %; gap to target; trend direction
Review cadence | Monthly / quarterly | Quarterly / bi-annually

The key insight: A team can complete every planned activity on time while the leader’s cumulative outcome trajectory is still off track. The leader is accountable for ensuring tasks are producing the outcomes the strategy requires.
When you last reviewed performance in your area, were you looking at team activities or at cumulative outcome trajectory? What would change if you shifted the focus?
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Reviewing Your Role When you last reviewed performance in your area, were you looking at team activities or at cumulative outcome trajectory? What would change if you shifted the focus? — In my last performance review I was mainly looking at... If I shifted to cumulative trajectory, I would see...

sections.label: Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where
sections.sub: Extending PM architecture to the enterprise level: how executive teams align their measurement signals, where execution gaps most commonly emerge, and how the industry is shifting.
slo: Recognise each executive role’s contribution to the evidence of enterprise progress.
Evaluate the execution gaps that prevent performance arrangements from supporting strategic priorities.

parts.title: 3.1 — The Alignment Brigade
content: At the enterprise level, the performance management system sits in the executive team. The C-suite is collectively the organisation’s measurement alignment system.

The Alignment Brigade concept recognises that each executive function carries a unique measurement responsibility — a “hot zone” of the enterprise they are best positioned to track, interpret, and act upon. When these hot zones are integrated through a shared cadence and common language, the executive team becomes a precision measurement system. When they operate independently, they produce competing narratives of organisational performance.
Write down what you believe are the top three enterprise performance priorities right now. Then compare with a colleague. What does any divergence reveal?
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Your Enterprise Signal Write down what you believe are the top three enterprise performance priorities right now. Then compare with a colleague. What does any divergence reveal? — My top 3 enterprise performance priorities right now: 1. 2. 3. What any divergence with colleagues reveals...

parts.title: 3.2 — CXO Hot Zones
content: Each executive function owns a distinct hot zone in the enterprise PM architecture. Explore your own role first, then the roles most adjacent to yours.

The CEO holds the integrated view of whether the organisation as a whole is on trajectory. The CEO’s PM role is to ensure the executive team is interpreting performance coherently and that the collective response is coordinated. The CEO is the only function with authority to enforce measurement alignment across all hot zones.

Enterprise trajectory signal — integrating all hot zones into a single coherent performance narrative. When this is absent: each function optimises its own metric at the expense of enterprise coherence.

The CFO interprets the financial performance signal: revenue, cost, margin, liquidity, and capital efficiency. In the PM context, the CFO translates financial data into strategic resource allocation signals — identifying where investment is producing returns and where it is absorbed without output.
Financial trajectory and investment return visibility. When this is absent: financial data becomes a constraint and loses its value as a strategic navigation tool.

The COO tracks the execution engine: throughput, cycle times, operational quality, and delivery consistency. The COO ensures operational performance rhythm is matched to strategic demand — the engine is running in the right direction at the right speed.
Operational rhythm and execution consistency. When this is absent: the organisation confuses motion with progress.

The CHRO tracks the capability and behaviour signal: talent pipeline health, performance distribution, leadership effectiveness, and cultural alignment. The CHRO ensures the organisation has the human capability to execute the strategy — and that behaviour is aligned to values as well as outcomes.
Capability pipeline and behavioural alignment. When this is absent: capability gaps become execution crises.

The CTO/CIO tracks system enablement: technology performance, digital capability, data quality, and system reliability. This function ensures technology is an execution accelerator. Poor system performance directly affects what people can deliver.
System performance and data reliability. When this is absent: teams are held accountable for gaps caused by system failures.

The CMO tracks brand perception, customer acquisition costs, pipeline health, campaign performance, and market share trajectory. The CMO provides the leading indicators of future revenue — the signal that tells the enterprise whether the market is responding to the strategy.
Market responsiveness and pipeline health. When this is absent: the enterprise acts on market signals that are already 3–6 months old.

The CCO tracks win rates, deal cycle times, customer retention, revenue per customer, and commercial pipeline conversion. The CCO translates commercial activity into revenue trajectory signals connecting market position to financial performance.
Revenue trajectory and commercial momentum. When this is absent: the organisation mistakes effort for momentum.

The CPO tracks supply reliability, product pipeline health, vendor performance, and input cost management. The CPO ensures the supply and product infrastructure can reliably support execution — that the organisation can deliver what it has committed to deliver.
Supply continuity and product pipeline. When this is absent: supply disruptions become execution crises that consume leadership capacity.

The CRO tracks regulatory compliance, risk appetite alignment, incident frequency, and control effectiveness. The CRO ensures strategic ambition is pursued within a coherent risk framework — enabling bold action without reckless exposure.
Risk alignment and governance integrity. When this is absent: risk appetite is interpreted differently across functions, creating asymmetric exposure.

The CSO tracks whether the organisation’s current activities, resource allocation, and performance trajectory are aligned to its multi-year strategic intent. The CSO provides the strategic integrity check — ensuring operational performance is not winning at the expense of strategic positioning.
Strategic coherence and portfolio alignment. When this is absent: operational urgency systematically erodes strategic intent over time.
Having explored your hot zone and the two most adjacent roles: what is the most important alignment conversation you need to have with an adjacent function in the next 30 days?
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Your Hot Zone Having explored your hot zone and the two most adjacent roles: what is the most important alignment conversation you need to have with an adjacent function in the next 30 days? — My hot zone is most aligned with... and most in tension with... The alignment conversation I need to have: ...

parts.title: 3.3 — The Three Execution Gaps
content: Three structural gaps account for the majority of PM system failures at the enterprise level.

Different functions use different definitions of what constitutes progress — finance says margin, operations says throughput, sales says pipeline. Without a unified definition of progress at the enterprise level, each function optimises its own metric at the expense of collective momentum.
Intervention: Agree on three to five metrics that, if achieved, confirm the strategy is working. Everything else becomes a supporting indicator.

The organisation is systematically not measuring something that matters. Common blind spots: cross-functional collaboration quality, leadership pipeline health, customer experience at key touchpoints. What is not measured is not managed — and eventually becomes a crisis.
Intervention: Map your measurement system against the Three Sights. Ask: “What would we need to see to know our strategy is working before the financial results confirm it?”
The incentive structure rewards behaviour inconsistent with the strategic intent. People follow the incentives. When incentives and strategy diverge, strategy loses. This is a design failure.
Intervention: Audit the current incentive structure against strategic priorities. Redesign to reward the behaviours the strategy actually requires.
Which of the three Execution Gaps is most present in your organisation right now? Why does it persist despite being understood?
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Your Dominant Gap Which of the three Execution Gaps is most present in your organisation right now? Why does it persist despite being understood? — The dominant gap in my organisation is Gap ___ because... It persists despite being understood because... The intervention I would prioritise: ...

parts.title: 3.4 — The Continuous PM Shift
content: 41% of organisations have moved to real-time or near-real-time feedback systems, replacing annual review cycles with continuous check-in models. This shift reflects a fundamental change in how high-performing organisations understand the relationship between feedback and performance.

The annual performance review is being supplemented or replaced by structured quarterly conversations, monthly check-ins, and continuous pulse feedback. Annual feedback is too infrequent to change behaviour and too delayed to be developmental.

Leading organisations are shifting from the rating (a backward-looking judgement) to development planning (a forward-looking investment). The rating becomes an input to development. Associated with higher engagement, stronger retention, and more rapid capability improvement.

Individual performance ratings are being complemented by team performance assessments. Most outcomes require coordinated contribution. Organisations that exclusively measure individual performance create hidden disincentives for collaboration.

sections.label: Section 4 · Integration — Collective
sections.sub: Synthesising awareness, intelligence, and context into an integrated enterprise PM design: the collective progress signal, the three elements of enterprise PM, and the EXECUTION framework.
slo: Define a shared enterprise signal of progress that anchors executive judgement.
Interpret cumulative progress to judge performance status and its strategic significance.

parts.title: 4.1 — The Collective Progress Signal
content: At the integration level, the executive team converges on a single shared question: are we collectively making progress toward our strategic intent? This Collective Progress Signal anchors three categories of executive question.
Execution Traction — Are we generating the expected progress?

Assesses whether the execution engine is producing results at the rate and quality the strategy requires. These are the most frequent questions in a well-functioning executive PM rhythm — the standing agenda item in every performance review. Risk: if only Traction questions are asked, the team optimises for current-period efficiency and loses sight of cumulative trajectory.
Execution Balance — Are we investing resources in the right proportions?

Steps back from individual metric performance to assess whether the portfolio of activity is balanced. High-performing organisations regularly discover that 80% of their resource is concentrated on the priority representing 30% of their strategic value — because that priority is most familiar or most politically visible.
Execution Intervention — Where must we intervene now?

The most consequential question in the executive PM dialogue. It moves from analysis to action: a specific decision about where leadership will direct energy, resources, or authority to recover a trajectory that is off track. Organisations that defer intervention decisions until the gap is irreversible have compliance PM systems masquerading as management systems.

parts.title: 4.2 — Three Elements of Enterprise PM Design
content: A complete enterprise PM design integrates three elements, each answering a different question at a different time horizon.
Defines the structured rhythm of the PM system: when performance is reviewed, by whom, and with what mandate. Without a defined cadence, performance management reverts to crisis management.
Monthly: Functional performance review; Periodic Measures
Quarterly: Enterprise PM review; Cumulative Progress; Intervention decisions
Annually: Full PM cycle review; rating calibration; system redesign

The performance data points collected and reviewed within each reporting period. They answer: What happened in this period? Periodic Measures must be Current, Comparable, and Actionable. A Periodic Measure that is only collected, never acted on, is a reporting cost with no management value.
The most strategically significant element and the most frequently absent. Answers: Across the full cycle, how far have we moved from baseline toward target?
Example: Complaint resolution: Baseline = 48 hrs, Target = 12 hrs, Current = 40 hrs.
A single-period improvement can mask a cumulative trajectory that is far behind target. At month 6 of 18, 22% complete means you are significantly behind the expected 33%.
Choose one current strategic priority. Calculate your cumulative progress percentage. What does the number tell you about whether you are on trajectory?
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Apply the Formula Choose one current strategic priority. Calculate your cumulative progress percentage. What does the number tell you about whether you are on trajectory? — Strategic priority: ... Baseline: ___ | Current: ___ | Target: ___ Cumulative Progress % = ___ What this tells me about trajectory: ...

parts.title: 4.3 — The EXECUTION Framework
content: The EXECUTION framework synthesises the nine design principles of a high-quality enterprise PM system. Rate your current PM system 1–5 against each principle. The lowest scores reveal your design priorities.
The PM system must be anchored to enterprise strategy. Every metric should be traceable to a strategic outcome.
Self-check: Can every metric in your PM system be traced back to a strategic priority?
Every individual must see a clear line of sight from their daily work to enterprise strategy. Without it, individuals execute their role description and lose sight of the strategy.
Self-check: Can every person on your team draw a line between their daily work and the strategy?
Performance assessments must be grounded in defined, agreed evidence. Without it, ratings are subjective and disputes are inevitable.
Self-check: Does your team know exactly what evidence is required to achieve each rating?
Accountability for results must be shared. Everyone with a contribution to an outcome has a stake in its measurement and a responsibility for its achievement.
Self-check: When a result is missed, does accountability sit with one person or is it genuinely shared?
The PM system must measure outcomes — the actual change produced. A team can be 100% active while producing 0% of the required outcome.
Self-check: If your team completed all planned activities this period, would outcomes automatically follow?
The logic by which performance is calculated, rated, and rewarded must be transparent to everyone subject to it. Hidden formulas and opaque scoring destroy confidence and generate cynicism.
Self-check: Does your team fully understand how their performance score is calculated?

The incentive structure must reward the behaviours and outcomes the strategy requires. When what gets rewarded diverges from what the strategy needs, people follow the incentive — this is a design failure.
Self-check: What behaviours does your incentive system actually reward? Do they match your strategy?
PM must be an ongoing rhythm. The review rhythm must be consistent and embedded in the operational calendar so that PM is how work is managed.
Self-check: Is PM embedded in how your team works week to week, or does it only surface at review time?

The ultimate function of a PM system is navigation: using performance data, collectively interpreted, to make better decisions about where to go and how to get there. A PM system that collects data but generates no collective insight is a reporting system dressed as management.
Self-check: In your last performance review, did you make a decision together that you would not have made individually?

sections.h2: MyHealth Live Portal — PM Design Simulation

content: Name one specific PM design change you will make in the next 30 days. Be specific: which FACES function, which EXECUTION principle, which Sight of Progress — and exactly what will change.

parts.title: 5.1 — Case Context: MyHealth Live Portal
content: Organisation: A hospital chain operating 12 facilities across three regions has approved a digital transformation initiative: the MyHealth Live Portal, a patient-facing platform enabling online appointment booking, real-time test results, and direct clinical communication.
Strategic Context: The portal is a strategic priority for the next 18 months. Three strategic outcomes have been defined:
Reduce patient complaint resolution time: 48 hrs → 12 hrs
Portal-based complaint submission and tracking live in all 12 facilities within 6 months; average resolution time below 12 hours within 12 months.
Reduce clinical referral decision time: 10 days → 3 days
Digital referral pathway active for 80% of non-urgent referral types within 9 months; average decision time below 3 days within 15 months.
Baseline: 30% of cases involve cross-facility input Target: 70%
Shared case management module live within 6 months; cross-facility consultation rate at or above 70% within 18 months.

content: Select the Periodic Measures that will be tracked monthly across the three strategic outcomes. Each must be Current, Comparable, and Actionable.

parts.title: 5.7 — Task 6 · Reporting Tool Design
content: Design the structure of the reporting tool that will support the MyHealth Live Portal PM system.
Executive Summary view: What does the CEO see on a single page that tells them whether the Portal strategy is on track?

parts.title: Unit Summary
content: “A performance management system that only measures has not yet become a management system. The moment measurement becomes the basis for a decision, a conversation, and an accountable intervention — that is the moment execution begins.”

A performance management system is an execution architecture. This unit equips you to design systems that translate strategy into individual accountability, calibrate progress rhythms, and sustain collective ownership.
Evaluate whether organisational performance arrangements support the achievement of strategic priorities.
Define clear relationships between enterprise outcomes, leadership accountability and performance evidence.
